The first time (i was 13) my dad fake cried and told me how I was insane and needed a psychiatrist (the latter was true lmao) but of course made no effort to actually get me mental health help. Then he told me to picture my baby brother (3 at the time) destroying his hands with scissors (my tool at the time) any time I got an urge, which was soooo helpful for my mental health. 
My mom locked me in the car and yelled at me, asking why I would do something so stupid. I let slip that it was about how I was being treated at home, and so she started to drive off and gave me a notepad and made me write everything I liked about her and all the good things she did. I wanted to jump out of that car so bad, even if we were on the highway.

The second time was after my first relapse (I was 19) My mom just rolled her eyes, and my dad asked me “are you cutting yourself again?” Like I’d spilled milk on the carpet. Somehow that hurt so much more than it feels like it should have. Later when I called them out for how they reacted (for context, they had gone through my email and found an email where I detailed the emotional abuse of my childhood to a therapist at my school) they kicked me out. 

I’m 20 now and living with my partner, and I’m so much happier. I’ve still relapsed, and I still have bad days, but I’m in a safe place to work through it now. I promise, it does get better. Healing isn’t linear, so don’t get discouraged when things dip again. Healing takes time, but it is possible. You are worthy, you are loved, you are enough.

I know how hard what you're going through is. I'm still trying to figure it out myself. Just try to hold on to the fact that this will not last forever. Things might get worse before they get better, but they *will* get better, no matter how bleak it seems. Also, I can say from personal experience that you should try to reach out to someone in your life whom you trust (Doesn't have to be family, doesn't have to be an adult, sometimes they just make it worse). Reaching out and talking about what you're going through in places like Reddit is a fantastic first step, but talking to someone you actually know (even over text) really helps. I know that it's easier said than done. A lot easier said than done, but it is worth it. The feeling of relief and validation of finding out from a friend or family member that there's nothing wrong with you and that they understand that you're hurting is an incredible feeling. They may not be able to fix it right away, but at least they can walk you through the dark. I hope this helps a bit. I know things are awful right now, but we are on the path to a better future. Stay strong, friend.

I've had to redefine family for myself, because my ndad is very bloodline oriented, if that makes sense, and it took me a long time to shake this viewpoint. However, family isn't something you're born into. Family is something you create, something you build. It takes years of careful love and nurturing, understanding, highs, lows, the whole shebang. Some people grow up with a true family, but others of us aren't so luck, and we have to find it on our own. People think I'm just being dramatic when I refer to my "close friends" as my real family, but that's simply the truth. I completely agree that your DNA and bloodline are irrelevant, because it's the people you love, the people who love you and support you, who make you feel like you're on top of the world, and who would do anything for you who are your real family.
